newsitem.title: USA: Coffee, soybeans drop on South American supplies.
newsitem.headline: Coffee, soybeans drop on South American supplies.

text.p: Coffee prices fell on Wednesday after Colombia said it would soon supply more coffee to world markets, while soybean prices dropped on news that Brazilian beans were being imported into the United States.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for July delivery closed 12.65 cents a pound lower at 251.55 cents.

Colombian Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said in a statement issued late on Tuesday that Colombia had opened "unlimited" export registrations for July to August shipment and expected to ship 2.5 million 132-pound bags during the period, welcome news for roasters now scrambling for beans.
"It is bearish because it implies there is more coffee available," said Refco Inc analyst Ann Prendergast. "And the market has been running up on tight supply."
But some analysts said the market may reacted too strongly since world stockpiles were still hovering near 20-year lows.

"I don't think it is as bearish as some people think," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "There is too much emphasis on the unlimited exports, but there might not be an unlimited amount of coffee to sell."

The market also remains nervous about the onset of winter in Brazil, with the memories of a damaging June 1994 frost in Brazil's coffee plantations -- and soaring prices -- still fresh. Brazil is the top coffee producer, Colombia number two.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean prices led grain markets lower. July soybeans closed down the 30-cent allowable daily limit at $8.30 a bushel after Minneapolis-based grain giant Cargill Inc said it was importing Brazilian soybeans.
U.S. soybean stocks are at the lowest levels in 20 years, and prices this spring have climbed to levels not seen since a Midwestern drought in 1988.

"Cargill has contracted to import soybeans from Brazil for use in our processing plants in the southeastern United States, where the (soybean) shortage is particularly acute," the company said in a statement.

"It's going to be negative for the cash market for a while because it takes away some premium," said Dale Durchholz, grain analyst with Agrivisor Services in Bloomington, Ill. "But total world consumption is still strong."

Futures prices on soybean meal, a livestock feed, also fell after Brazilian processor Ceval Ailmentos said it was in talks to sell 40,000 metric tons of the meal to an unnamed buyer in the United States, which traders said likely a large hog producer on the East Coast.
July soymeal closed down the $10 a ton daily limit at $273.10 a ton.
The heavy selloff in soybeans pressured corn prices, as did excellent growing weather in the Midwest for the young corn crop. July corn ended 6-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $2.71-1/4.
Wheat prices also slid to three-month lows, with July wheat closing down 8-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.53-3/4.

Harvest progress in Texas was adding to supplies, with combines in wheat fields as far north as Fort Worth. Forecasts for a dry week in Oklahoma and Texas suggested harvest would continue at a rapid clip, traders said.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil prices fell for a second straight day with supply-demand fundamentals overcoming the more speculative buying of recent sessions.

Crude oil for July delivery fell 21 cents to end at $20.12 a barrel, while July unleaded gasoline fell 1.02 cents to end at 60.42 cents a gallon and July heating oil shed 0.46 cent to end at 54.16 cents a gallon.

The United Nations Security Council, as expected, on Wednesday approved renewal of a six-month deal allowing Iraq to sell oil to obtain food and supplies, a move that should keep world oil markets well stocked.
A weekly report from the American Petroleum Institute issued late on Tuesday also showed steadily rising inventories in crude and products in the United States.
Jim Ritterbusch, a trader at Sweeney Oil in Chicago, said market fundamentals were carrying the day.

"They are decidedly bearish," he said. "At some point we've got to look at this evolving situation and say, 'Wow, crude stocks are building in the midst of the highest refinery usage we've seen in two years.'"
